question: A 62-year-old man presents with two episodes of painless, bright red urine. He has no dysuria, fever, or loin pain. Dipstick confirms haematuria. What is the single most important next step?

answers.text: Prescribe a course of antibiotics and review in two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antibiotic therapy is not indicated without evidence of infection; delaying cancer investigation in painless haematuria is dangerous.

answers.text: Arrange urgent flexible cystoscopy and upper-tract imaging (CT urogram)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Painless visible haematuria in a man over 40 is bladder cancer until proven otherwise; urgent two-part haematuria work-up (cystoscopy + upper-tract CT) is mandatory.

answers.text: Repeat the urine dipstick in four weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surveillance dipstick is appropriate only for asymptomatic non-visible haematuria; a visible episode in this age group demands immediate investigation.

answers.text: Request a PSA and rectal examination for prostate cancer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Prostate cancer rarely causes visible haematuria; the priority here is cystoscopy to exclude bladder cancer and imaging to exclude renal/urothelial tumour.

overallFeedback.feedback: Painless visible haematuria is a red-flag symptom. Antibiotics and watchful waiting are never first-line; urgent two-part haematuria investigation is required.
Well done. Painless haematuria in a man over 40 — cystoscopy plus CT urogram is the standard two-component work-up.
